title: The third wave that was not launched
question:
By the early afternoon of 7 December the aircraft were back aboard, the American battle line was wrecked, the defence was disorganised and there were hours of daylight left. Untouched were the fuel tank farms, the submarine base and the repair shops — the things that made Pearl Harbor a fleet base rather than a lagoon. Nagumo turned north and went home.

Should he have struck a third time? Would it have changed the war if he had? And — the question underneath both — did anybody aboard actually propose it?

The three questions are usually run together, which is how the argument has stayed alive. They come apart when the evidence for each is looked at separately — and the first thing to say is that the operation order contains no third wave at all, so whatever was proposed on that bridge was a departure from the plan and not the execution of it.

positions.label: The chance that was thrown away
positions.who: Gordon Prange, *At Dawn We Slept* (1981), and Edwin Layton, *“And I Was There”* (1985) — Layton was fleet intelligence officer to Kimmel and then to Nimitz, and it is through him that Nimitz's own remark on the fuel is usually quoted
positions.summary:
On this reading the attack was a tactical triumph and a strategic half-measure. Battleships, the argument runs, could be raised, patched and put back into the line; the fuel oil sitting in unprotected surface tanks — four and a half million barrels of it, in the figure the argument usually names and which this pack could not verify — could not be replaced from anywhere nearer than California, and the dry docks and machine shops that repaired the fleet could not be replaced at all. Destroy those, and the Pacific Fleet has to withdraw to the American west coast and fight the next year of the war two thousand miles further back. Nimitz is quoted as saying it would have prolonged the war by two years.

**This position is stated at second hand and the pack says so.** Neither volume could be opened from this project's environment — every Internet Archive copy is a lending copy — so nothing here is inside quotation marks, no page is given, and the argument is described as its opponents and the general literature describe it rather than in its authors' own words. That is a real weakness in this card and it is written here rather than hidden. See *What has not been read*.

positions.label: There was no third wave to launch
positions.who: Alan Zimm, *Attack on Pearl Harbor: Strategy, Combat, Myths, Deceptions* (2011)
positions.summary:
The counter-case is that the question is built on a premise that does not survive contact with the plan. No third strike was in the operation order; the Japanese navy paid very little attention to logistics in its own planning and had no reason to be thinking about anybody else's; the aircrew were trained, briefed and armed for warships; and oil tanks are a harder target for a 250-kilogram bomb than the argument assumes — they burn, they do not evaporate, and they are refilled from tankers. A third strike, on this reading, would have flown into an alerted defence and achieved minor damage against a base that would have been working again shortly.

**Also stated at second hand.** No copy of Zimm could be opened from here. What was read is a signed review of it by Charles C. Kolb for the Naval Historical Foundation, which sets out these conclusions and from which the bibliographic detail in the registry entry also comes.

positions.label: The proposal itself is a postwar invention
positions.who: Jonathan Parshall, “Reflecting on Fuchida, or ‘A Tale of Three Whoppers’”, *Naval War College Review* (2010), and with Anthony Tully in *Shattered Sword* (2005)
positions.summary:
This position is about the evidence rather than the outcome, which is why it is the one that can be checked from here. The story of a conference on *Akagi*'s bridge at which Fuchida urged a third strike against the fuel installations and was refused comes from Fuchida, and Parshall shows that it grew in the telling. In the interview Prange took in 1948, Fuchida's priorities for a further strike were the damaged battleships first, the ships in the navy yard second, and the “all important installations, oil tanks, etc.” third — which, as Parshall puts it, “puts fuel tanks dead last on the list” and is broadly what his actual briefed targets had been. By 1963 he was telling Prange that on the flight back he “also had his mind on the destruction of U.S. fuel reserves” and had earmarked “occasional ships, the naval and dock yards and the fuel tanks”.

Parshall's structural point is the stronger one: “Fuel tanks and logistical vessels did not fit their mental models”, and he quotes Evans and Peattie's *Kaigun* on an officer corps for whom the problems of bullets, beans and black oil “could not hold the attention of either staff or line officers”. A navy that did not think that way about its own supply did not think that way about the enemy's.

This is the same witness whose Midway testimony *Shattered Sword* dismantled, and it is why this pack cites Fuchida as a subject and never as an authority. **Read at one remove but in the historian's own words:** the journal's PDF returns 403 to this environment, and the sentences quoted here are from Parshall's own restatement of the argument on combinedfleet.com.

positions.label: He had a reason that needs no third wave at all
positions.who: The Green Books' account of the day (Louis Morton, *Strategy and Command*, 1962), and the standard operational reading that follows from it
positions.summary:
The simplest explanation of the withdrawal does not require anyone to have proposed anything. Three American carriers and their escorts were at sea and Nagumo did not know where they were. His own aircraft strength was down, his fuel had to last him home across three thousand miles, and he had achieved what he had been sent to achieve. Staying inside range of an enemy whose carriers are unlocated, to attack shore installations he had not been briefed for, would have been a different operation from the one he had been given.

On this reading the third-wave debate is a question about 1945 and after, not about the bridge of *Akagi* on the afternoon of the 7th — and the interesting historical fact is not that Nagumo declined a third strike but that nobody in Tokyo had thought to order one.

settled:
Four things are not in dispute. The fuel tank farms, the submarine base and the repair facilities were not attacked and were not damaged. The operation order contains no third wave: what it allows is repeated attacks if the destruction of enemy air strength “progresses favorably”, which is a contingency about air superiority. The striking force withdrew, as that same order said it would, once the second wave had been launched. And the three American carriers were at sea.

One number often quoted alongside this argument is **not** settled and this pack will not print it as a fact. The figure of four and a half or six million barrels at Pearl Harbor is repeated everywhere; the Navy's own construction history gives no capacity at all for the two above-ground tank farms that existed in 1941, and the six-million-barrel figure it does give belongs to the *underground* storage project, begun in December 1940, whose first vault was not usable until September 1942. Whatever was in the tanks on 7 December 1941, this pack could not find a source it could open that says how much.
unread:
This card is thinner than it looks and the reason is worth stating plainly.

**Only one of its four positions is quoted from its holder.** Parshall's is, at one remove — the journal article itself is unreachable from this environment and the sentences are from his own restatement of it on his website. Prange and Layton, who hold the position the whole argument is named for, could not be opened at all: every copy is a lending copy, so their case is described here as others describe it, which is not good enough and is not pretended to be. Zimm is in the same position, reached through a signed review.

What would raise this card: the three volumes at page level; Goldstein and Dillon's *The Pearl Harbor Papers* (1993), which prints the Japanese planning documents in translation and is the nearest thing to a primary set for the operation; and the Prange interview transcripts of 1948 and 1963 that Parshall works from, which are the actual evidence under the whole third-wave story and which nobody arguing about it on either side has been able to put in front of a general reader.

Also unread here, and it matters: nothing Japanese. The *Senshi Sōsho* volume covering the Hawaii operation is untranslated, and the monograph this pack does use is itself a postwar reconstruction from memory.
